clue.text: Academic point of view produces sympathy

blocks.note: a fellow is a senior member of a college or university
a feeling about something is an opinion or point of view

explanation.surface: A scholar's particular outlook turns out to generate compassion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Academic' looks like an adjective qualifying 'point of view', but it is a noun for a college member.
explanation.definitionFit: Fellow feeling is the shared understanding of another person's situation, a close synonym for compassion or empathy.

clue.text: Fussier tailoring producing slit

indicators.note: tailoring cuts and reshapes material, so the letters are refashioned into a new form

explanation.surface: A fussier approach to sewing results in a slit in the garment.
explanation.walkthrough: The tailoring image makes 'slit' sound like a cut in cloth; here it is just a crack or narrow opening.
explanation.definitionFit: A fissure is a long narrow crack or opening, the same thing as a slit in rock or tissue.

clue.text: Catalogue includes unknown composer

indicators.note: to include something is to take it inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: algebraic unknowns are x, y and z

explanation.surface: A record label's catalogue features a little-known composer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unknown composer' reads as one phrase, but 'unknown' is a separate piece: the letter used for an unknown quantity.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz Liszt was the nineteenth-century Hungarian pianist who wrote the Hungarian Rhapsodies.

clue.text: Wore pants with gut that's got too big for?

indicators.note: pants is British slang for rubbish, so these letters are in a hopeless jumbled state

explanation.surface: Someone wore trousers over a belly that had expanded beyond them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pants' looks like trousers worn over the gut; in British slang it means poor or rubbish, signalling a jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: To outgrow clothes is to become too large for them, exactly what getting too big for means.

clue.text: Loyal staff running with baton in team-building exercise

indicators.note: something running is in motion and on the move, so the letters move into a new order

explanation.surface: Faithful employees carry a relay baton during a corporate away-day activity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Team-building exercise' suggests office bonding; read literally, it is a game in which you pick your own imaginary team of real players.
explanation.definitionFit: In this game each player assembles a squad of real footballers and scores points from their performances, literally constructing a side.

clue.text: Fixtures in north taken on by northbound Redgrave?

indicators.note: in a down entry, heading toward the top of the grid means reading upwards, so the order runs backwards
to be taken on is to be absorbed or hired into something, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: Sir Steve Redgrave, the five-time Olympic champion rower

explanation.surface: Matches in the north are taken on by a Redgrave heading up the country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Redgrave' calls to mind the acting family, Vanessa or Michael; the rower's first name is the one needed.
explanation.definitionFit: Sporting fixtures are scheduled occasions such as races or matches, which are events on a programme.

clue.text: Dramatist not beginning his work, 'Give And Take'

indicators.note: lacking a beginning means the opening letter is dropped

blocks.note: Harold Pinter, the playwright, minus his first letter
a dramatist's work is a play

explanation.surface: A playwright has yet to start his new piece, entitled 'Give And Take'.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks and capitals dress the definition up as a play title, tying it to the dramatist.
explanation.definitionFit: Interplay is mutual action and reaction between parties, the reciprocal exchange described by give-and-take.

clue.text: Some detecting rat in some French dishes

indicators.note: taking only some of the following text means the letters sit inside it

blocks.note: runs from the end of the first word into the start of the last

explanation.surface: Some people spot a rodent in certain French meals.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'Some' is the signal; the second 'some' belongs to the letters being searched.
explanation.definitionFit: A gratin is a French dish topped with breadcrumbs or cheese and browned under a grill.

clue.text: Post-It's regularly showing trident shapes

indicators.note: at regular intervals means every other letter is kept

blocks.note: first, third, fifth and seventh letters

explanation.surface: Sticky notes routinely display little pitchfork doodles.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen and apostrophe are ignored; only the letters count.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek letter psi is drawn like Neptune's three-pronged spear, so these letters are trident-shaped characters.

clue.text: Bungling tail captures spy concealing note that's irrelevant

indicators.note: a bungled job is botched and muddled, so these letters come out in a mess
to capture is to seize and hold, so one piece wraps around another
to conceal is to hide inside, so a piece goes within another

blocks.note: a spy is a secret agent

explanation.surface: A clumsy shadow catches a spy hiding a message that turns out not to matter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tail' suggests someone following the spy; it is just four letters to rearrange. Two containers nest: one letter inside the spy, the spy inside the reordered word.
explanation.definitionFit: A tangential remark only touches the subject at one point, so it is peripheral and beside the point.

clue.text: One might add fine powder; more often, one removes it

definitions.text: One might add fine powder; more often, one removes it

blocks.note: surface reading: a shaker for sprinkling icing sugar or cocoa over a cake
setter's reading: the more familiar cloth for wiping fine particles off furniture

explanation.walkthrough: The verb 'dust' means both to sprinkle powder on and to wipe powder off; the noun covers both tools.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a household cloth for cleaning surfaces and also a kitchen shaker for sprinkling sugar.

clue.text: A performance-enhancing drug for a flier

blocks.note: anabolic steroids are banned performance-enhancers in sport

explanation.surface: A banned substance taken by a pilot or athlete to boost performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flier' suggests a pilot or sprinter who might dope; it is a rocky body hurtling through space.
explanation.definitionFit: An asteroid is a small rocky body orbiting the sun, so it is something that travels through space.

clue.text: However casually learner is given direction, styles ensue

blocks.note: L for learner, as on L-plates
styles or manners of doing something

explanation.surface: A trainee driver is told which way to go, and various approaches follow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Casually' marks the definition as informal: the answer is a colloquial alternative to 'at least' or 'however'.
explanation.definitionFit: Leastways is an informal or dialect word used to qualify a statement, much like saying anyway or at any rate.

clue.text: Revolutionary operatives losing power: it ended with glasnost

indicators.note: to lose something is to be left without it, so a letter drops out
a revolution overturns the established order, so the letters are overturned too

blocks.note: P is the physics symbol for power

explanation.surface: Communist agents lose their influence in the period that closed with Gorbachev's openness policy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' fits the Bolshevik theme perfectly, which hides its role as the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Gorbachev's policy of openness in the late 1980s preceded the collapse of the USSR, closing that historical period.

clue.text: Misfortune: Everyman is going to speechify at the opening

definitions.note: the answer is plural; misfortune here is a mass noun

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter, so only that is kept

blocks.note: the setter speaks of himself as I, and 'I am going to' contracts to I'll

explanation.surface: The setter laments his bad luck and announces he'll make a speech about it at the start.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often refer to themselves by name, so 'Everyman' stands for the first person; the apostrophe of the contraction is dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: Ills are troubles, harms or hardships, which together amount to adversity and bad luck.

clue.text: Seamen like part of a church, we're told?

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it spoken, so the sound matters rather than spelling

blocks.note: the nave is the main body of a church, and -y makes it 'resembling a nave'

explanation.surface: Sailors are compared to a section of a church building.
explanation.walkthrough: The suffix -y turns a noun into an adjective meaning 'like it', so a made-up word meaning nave-like is heard.
explanation.definitionFit: A country's navy is its body of sailors and warships, a collective term for seamen.

clue.text: Tense following refusal. Little drink? Absolutely

indicators.note: coming after something means placed behind it in the sequence

blocks.note: T is the grammar abbreviation for tense
a half is half a pint of beer in a British pub

explanation.surface: Someone nervous after being turned down is offered a small drink and eagerly accepts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tense' looks like an adjective for the person refused; it is the grammatical term. NOT HALF is British slang for an emphatic yes.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang 'not half!' is an emphatic agreement meaning very much so or certainly.

clue.text: Genova resort with boy making safe journey

indicators.note: read as re-sort, it means arrange again, so the letters are put in a different order

explanation.surface: A lad travelling to an Italian holiday town is wished a good trip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resort' pairs naturally with the Italian city as a holiday destination; split as re-sort, it signals rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase is said to someone setting out, wishing them a pleasant and safe trip.

clue.text: From advert, I got a queasy feeling

indicators.note: taking something from within a phrase means extracting a run of its letters

blocks.note: runs across the three words, ignoring the comma

explanation.surface: A television advertisement made someone feel sick.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters stop one short of the end of 'got', which stops the reader from seeing a whole-word break.
explanation.definitionFit: Vertigo is a spinning, dizzy sensation that often brings nausea, so it is a sickly sensation of imbalance.

clue.text: What gingery may become?

indicators.note: becoming something means changing form, so the letters change into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A question about what a redhead's hair might turn into over the years.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: the letters of the red-haired word rearrange, and red hair does literally turn grey with age.
explanation.definitionFit: Hair that is reddish in youth loses its colour over time, turning silver or white as a person ages.

clue.text: Supremely ethereal, revered angel playing horn, primarily?

definitions.text: Supremely ethereal, revered angel playing horn

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so the opening letter of each word is kept

blocks.clueFragment: Supremely ethereal, revered angel playing horn

explanation.surface: A heavenly being of the highest order plays a celestial trumpet.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes the answer while its initials spell it; seraphim are the highest order of angels.
explanation.definitionFit: A seraph belongs to the highest rank of angels in Christian tradition, a heavenly and venerated celestial being.

clue.text: Most expensive horse doesn't finish – bother!

indicators.note: not reaching the end means the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: a steed is a horse; its last letter goes
to pester or bother; a pest is a bother

explanation.surface: The priciest racehorse fails to complete the race, to its owner's annoyance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Steep' is informal for overpriced, so the superlative means priciest. 'Bother!' reads as an exclamation; it is a noun for a nuisance.
explanation.definitionFit: Steep is informal for excessively costly, so the superlative describes the highest price of all.

clue.text: Greek island reportedly closes?

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so only the sound counts

blocks.note: in Britain a close is a short dead-end residential street

explanation.surface: A Greek island seems to be shutting its doors for the season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Closes' looks like a verb, as if the island shuts; it is the British noun for a cul-de-sac street.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhodes is the largest of the Dodecanese islands in the Aegean, home of the ancient Colossus.

clue.text: Yemeni's neighbour soon to be rising

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means reading from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: 'in a mo' is informal British for in a moment, soon

explanation.surface: A person from Yemen will shortly be getting up from their seat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soon' has to become a three-word phrase, 'in a mo', short for in a moment.
explanation.definitionFit: Oman shares a border with Yemen on the Arabian Peninsula, so a citizen of Oman lives next door.

clue.text: Walk Amelia round body of water

indicators.note: turning things round moves them about, so the letters are moved into a different order

explanation.surface: An instruction to take a woman for a stroll around a pond or lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' reads as walking around the water; it is the signal to rearrange the first two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Lake Malawi is a vast African Great Lake bordering Malawi, Mozambique and Tanzania.

clue.text: Enclosed by what pyramids must enclose

indicators.note: whatever a word encloses is inside it, so the letters are within the next word

explanation.surface: A riddle about what lies sealed inside the Egyptian tombs.
explanation.walkthrough: It sounds like asking about burial chambers or mummies; the answer is literally spelt inside the word, and is itself a word meaning 'surrounded by'.
explanation.definitionFit: Amid is a preposition meaning in the middle of or surrounded by, matching being encircled by something.

clue.text: Battered half of old sign seen in cataclysmic weather

indicators.note: something battered is beaten out of shape, so the letters are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: Half an old signpost, knocked about, is spotted during a violent storm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half of' invites taking half the letters of a word, but every letter of 'half of old sign' is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Flash flooding is the sudden inundation caused by torrential rain, a destructive and dangerous meteorological event.
